password.title: Password generator
password.summary: Create a strong, random password, passphrase or PIN. It is made in your browser and never leaves it.
password.description: Free password generator: strong random passwords and PINs made in your browser with a cryptographic random source. Nothing is sent or saved.
password.avoid: Leave out look-alikes (0 O o, 1 l I |)
password.noSets: Choose at least one kind of character.
password.note1: Every character is picked with your browser's cryptographic random generator, the same source used for encryption keys. The password exists only on this page: it is not saved or sent, and it is gone when you close the tab.
password.note2: Save the password in a password manager straight away, and use a different one for every account. Length matters more than symbols: 16 random characters or more is enough for almost anything.
password.note3: A PIN made of digits is much weaker than a password of the same length. Use one only where a PIN is required, such as a phone or SIM lock, and prefer six digits or more. Without a limit on tries, a computer can go through every possible PIN quickly. A phone that locks after a few wrong tries makes a PIN much safer than that.
password.time: Time to guess at a trillion tries a second: {time}
password.ai1: Don't ask an AI chatbot to make up a password. Language models write text that looks random but follows patterns, so their passwords are easier to guess than they seem, and the password then sits in your chat history on someone else's servers. A generator like this one uses your device's cryptographic random source and keeps the result on this page.
password.pinCodes: There are {codes} possible codes of this length. A computer tries them all at once, so a PIN is only as safe as the lock that limits guessing.
password.pinLockout: If the device stops accepting guesses after {tries} wrong tries, the chance of guessing it is 1 in {odds}.
password.note4: The passphrase words come from EFF’s long word list (Electronic Frontier Foundation, CC BY 4.0). Six random words are about as strong as a 13-character random password of letters and digits, and much easier to type and remember.

links.title: Link cleaner
links.summary: Paste a link and get it back without the tracking parts, before you share it.
links.description: Remove tracking parameters such as utm_source and fbclid from a link before you share it. Works in your browser: the link is never opened or sent anywhere.
links.input: Paste a link, or a message with links
links.clean: No tracking parts that this tool knows of were found. It can only recognise the ones on its list.
links.invalid: No web link was found. A link looks like https://example.com/page or example.com/page.
links.unwrapped: This link went through {host} first. That detour is removed too.
links.note1: Links copied from Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, newsletters and ads often carry extra parts such as fbclid or utm_source. They tell the site who shared the link or which ad was clicked, and can connect your account to the people you send it to.
links.note2: The tool only edits the text of the link. It never opens the link and never contacts the site, so nobody learns that you checked it.
links.note3: Short links such as bit.ly or t.co can't be cleaned this way: only the shortening service knows the real address. Open them only if you trust the sender.
links.exampleText: Have a look: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=abc123XYZ00&si=AbCdEf123GhIj and the shop: https://example.com/product?id=42&utm_source=facebook&utm_campaign=sale&fbclid=IwAR2xYz#:~:text=only%20today
links.shared: {host} share links like this one are tied to the account that made them: {host} says it can suggest the account to whoever opens the link. Nothing in such a link can be removed here. Open it yourself, then copy the address the page shows and clean that instead.
links.lookup: This is a {host} share link: {host} looks up the real address only when it is opened, so nothing in it can be seen or removed here. Share links can be tied to the account that made them. Open it yourself, then copy the address the page shows and clean that instead.
links.short: {host} is a short link: the address it leads to isn’t written in it, so it can’t be seen or cleaned here. Open it yourself, then copy the address the page shows and clean that instead.
links.email: This link contains an email address ({list}): anyone you send it to can read it. It is left in, because the page may need it.
links.secret: This link has a part that looks like a sign-in or access code ({list}). Anyone who gets the link may be able to get into the account. It is left in, because the page may need it: think twice before sharing it.

photo.description: Check what hidden data a photo carries (location, date, phone model) and save a clean copy. The photo is read in your browser and never uploaded.
photo.file: Choose photos (JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIC or AVIF)
photo.found: Hidden data found in this photo:
photo.none: No hidden data found in this photo.
photo.unsupported: This file type isn't supported. Choose a JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIC or AVIF photo.
photo.compact: This photo uses a newer, compact HEIF layout that this tool can't read yet, so nothing was checked. Save it as JPEG and check that copy.
photo.tooLarge: This file is too large. The limit is 40 MB.
photo.damaged: This file couldn't be read. It may be damaged.
photo.verified: Checked: the clean copy was read again and contains none of the removed data.
photo.verifyFailed: The clean copy didn't pass the check, so it isn't offered. Save the photo as JPEG and check that copy.
photo.previewLabel: Preview picture stored in the file
photo.previewCaption: The preview picture stored inside the file. If the photo was cropped or edited, the preview can still show the original.

kept.thumbnail: The preview picture: HEIC and AVIF store it as a separate picture, which this tool can't remove.
kept.xmp: Editing details (XMP) stored in a way this tool can't read or remove.
kept.exif: Camera details (EXIF) stored in a way this tool can't read or remove.
kept.other: Other data this tool can't remove from HEIC and AVIF files, such as a video.

photo.keptHow: To remove these too, save the photo as JPEG and check that copy here.

flags.exif: Lens, exposure and other technical details
flags.iptc: Other descriptive details (IPTC), for example dates or categories
flags.photoshop: Data saved by Photoshop or another editing program
flags.comment: A text comment saved inside the file
flags.thumbnail: A small copy of the photo, which can show it as it was before cropping
flags.trailing: Data after the image, for example the video of a motion photo
flags.c2pa: A signed record of how the picture was made and edited (C2PA). It can include a copy of the details above and a small copy of the picture.
flags.hdr: An HDR layer that makes the photo brighter on some screens. The clean copy shows the ordinary picture without it.
flags.other: Other data that isn't needed to show the picture
flags.unread: Camera or editing data that this tool couldn’t read to the end. It may hold a location or names; the clean copy leaves it out.

why.location: Anyone with the file can put this on a map.
why.serial: The same in every photo from this camera, so it can link your photos to each other.
why.lensSerial: The same in every photo taken with this lens, so it can link your photos to each other.
why.uniqueId: It can link this photo to its other copies.
why.texts: AI image tools store the prompt and settings here; other programs store notes.
why.profile: A profile made for one screen, or by one person, can name them.

photo.note1: Phones save more than the picture: often the exact place, the time and the phone model. Anyone who gets the original file can read them.
photo.note2: The photo is opened in your browser only. It is not uploaded, and this site can't see it. You can check: the tool keeps working with the internet turned off.
photo.note3: The clean copy is the same picture, not compressed again, so the quality doesn’t change. Rotation and colour information stay, so it looks the same; a standard colour profile (sRGB, Display P3, Adobe RGB) is replaced with a plain one of the same kind. Everything else is removed. A few things can’t be removed from HEIC and AVIF photos, and a colour profile that isn’t a standard one stays unless you remove it: the report says when they stay.
photo.note4: Messengers usually remove this data when you send a picture as a photo, but not when you send it as a file or document. Email and many websites keep it. Removing metadata doesn't hide what the picture itself shows: faces, street signs, screens.
photo.note5: Videos aren’t covered: this tool reads photos only. Cleaning a JPEG with an HDR or depth layer keeps the ordinary picture and drops the extra layers.
photo.pasteHint: You can also paste a photo or drop several files here.
photo.ai1: Removing metadata is no longer the whole story. AI models can often work out where a photo was taken from the picture alone: the buildings, signs, plants, even the light. If the place must stay private, check what is visible in the background, not only what is stored in the file.
photo.ai2: If you upload a photo to an AI chatbot, the service receives the original file, hidden data included. Clean it first if the place or time matters.
photo.optimised: This PNG is in a form made for iPhone apps (Apple’s CgBI), which browsers can’t show, so this tool can’t clean it.
photo.batchLimit: Not checked: the photos chosen together are larger than 200 MB. Check this one on its own.
photo.dropProfile: Remove it too (colours may look slightly different)
photo.verifiedMetadataOnly: Checked: the clean copy’s data was read again and contains none of the removed data. This browser can’t show this kind of picture, so the picture itself wasn’t checked.

video.summary: See what a video says about where and when it was recorded and on which device, and save a copy without it.
video.description: Remove location, recording time and device details from MP4 and MOV videos in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and the quality stays the same.
video.file: Choose a video (MP4, MOV, M4V or 3GP)
video.fileHint: The video is read on your device and never uploaded. Long videos work too: only the parts that hold these details are read, not the picture and sound.
video.none: No location, time or device details found in this video.

errors.unsupported: This tool can’t read this file. It reads MP4, MOV, M4V and 3GP videos, the formats phones and many cameras record in.
errors.photo: This is a photo (HEIC or AVIF), not a video. The photo metadata remover can clean it.
errors.damaged: This video looks damaged or incomplete, so it can’t be cleaned safely. Nothing was changed.
errors.tooLarge: The part of this video that lists its contents is too large for this tool to read. Nothing was changed.
errors.fragmented: This video was saved in fragments, and this tool can’t clean the data inside them. Nothing was changed.
errors.readFailed: The browser couldn’t read the file. If the video is stored online, download it to your device first and try again.

flags.emptyLocation: A location field without a position (0, 0). It is removed too.
flags.thumbnail: A small picture saved with the video. It can show a frame you cut out or didn’t mean to share.
flags.c2pa: A signed record of how the video was made and edited (C2PA)
flags.cameraData: Records the camera keeps about itself, such as IDs
flags.samsung: Extra data that Samsung phones add to their videos
flags.frameData: The date, time and camera settings and, on some cameras, the GPS position and serial number, stored with every frame
flags.timecode: A time code, which can hold the time of day the recording started
flags.dataTrack: Data recorded alongside the picture, such as motion sensors. This tool can’t read all of it; the copy has it emptied.
flags.gpsLog: A GPS log that the camera maker keeps in a format of its own
flags.hiddenData: Data in space the file marks as empty. Some cameras keep their GPS log there.
flags.trackNames: Names of the parts of the file, which can tell which phone, camera or app made it
flags.other: Other details stored in the file

why.location: Anyone with the file can put this on a map.
why.route: A position for every moment of filming: where you were and which way you went.
why.serial: The same in every video from this camera, so it can link your videos to each other.
why.lensSerial: The same in every video taken with this lens, so it can link your videos to each other.
why.uniqueId: It can link this video to its other copies, or to the photo taken with it.
why.fileName: Some phones and cameras name files after the date and time of recording.

video.routeUnread: Positions stored with the video ({n} entries). This tool can’t show them, but the clean copy has them removed.

left.encoderName: The name of the encoder, part of the video settings that players read
left.subtitles: Subtitles or other text tracks, which can hold any text, including a position. Check them before you share
left.unknownBox: Parts of the file this tool doesn’t know

video.stays: This tool doesn’t change what the video shows and records: faces, voices, signs, number plates and the place. Cut or cover them before you share. A clean copy isn’t anonymous.
video.verified: Checked: the clean copy was read again and holds none of the removed details. The picture and sound are unchanged.
video.verifyFailed: The clean copy didn’t pass the check, so it isn’t offered.
video.note1: Phones and cameras save more than the picture in a video file: often the exact place, the time and the device. Action cameras and drones can record a whole GPS route, with a position for every moment of filming.
video.note2: The video is read in your browser only. It isn’t uploaded, and this site can’t see it. Only the parts of the file that hold these details are read, not the picture and sound, so long videos work too, even on a phone.
video.note3: The clean copy is the same video. Nothing is encoded again, so the picture and sound don’t change and the file keeps its size: the details are overwritten with zeros. The copy is read again before it is offered.
video.note4: Google says that Google Photos can’t remove a location your camera added, and that copies you download and send elsewhere, for example by email, keep the original location. Clean the file itself before you share it.
video.note5: To stop new photos and videos from recording where you are, see the guide on location and photos. If you may need the original later, for example as evidence, keep it safe and share only the clean copy.
video.ai1: Uploading a video to an online metadata remover or to an AI service hands the original file to whoever runs that service: its location, and the faces and voices in it. This tool reads the file on your device instead.

attachment.title: Attachment checker
attachment.summary: Find out what a file you received really is, and whether opening it can run something.
attachment.description: Check a file before you open it: is it a program, is it disguised, does it hold macros or scripts? It is read in your browser and never uploaded.
attachment.fileHint: Any kind of file; you can choose several. They are read on your device, never opened, run or uploaded.
attachment.capped: Only the first {max} files were checked.
attachment.limit: This tool can’t tell whether a file is harmful, only whether it can run something or pretends to be something else. It isn’t an antivirus.

verdicts.program: Opening this can run a program on your device.
verdicts.disguise: This file pretends to be something it isn’t.
verdicts.active: When opened, this file can run code, fetch something or show a fake page.
verdicts.locked: Part of this file couldn’t be checked.

advice.program: Don’t open it unless you asked for exactly this file and trust where it came from. If you know the sender, ask them in another way whether they really sent it.
advice.disguise: Files are disguised like this so that people open them. Don’t open it, and ask the sender in another way whether they really sent it.
advice.active: Don’t enable macros, content or editing, and don’t type a password into a page that opens from a file. If you weren’t expecting this file, ask the sender in another way.
advice.locked: A file the tool can’t look into can still hide something. If you weren’t expecting it, ask the sender in another way before you open it.
advice.none: That isn’t a guarantee: this tool doesn’t know every trick, and a file can be harmful in other ways. If you weren’t expecting this file, ask the sender in another way.

attachment.linkOk: No warning signs in this address.
attachment.linkWarn: The link checker has warnings about this address: {n}.
attachment.linksHint: To see the warnings, paste a link into the

findings.script: It’s a script: text that the system runs as a program when you open it.
findings.installer: It’s a Windows Installer package. Opening it installs software.
findings.androidApp: It’s an Android app from outside Google Play. Don’t install it unless you trust where it came from.
findings.javaApp: It’s a Java program. Opening it runs it on a computer with Java installed.
findings.profile: It’s an Apple configuration profile. Installing it changes your device’s settings; one installed by mistake can be removed in Settings > General > VPN & Device Management. It sets up:
findings.shortcut: It’s a shortcut. Opening it runs or opens what it points to:
findings.riskyExtension: Files with this ending run as programs or scripts, or install or open something. Gmail or Outlook block them as attachments:
findings.riskyOpen: Files with this ending open or install something, such as a certificate, a theme or a remote folder. Gmail or Outlook block them as attachments:
findings.bidi: The name contains invisible characters that reverse part of it and hide the real ending. Written out, and as it may look:
findings.doubleExtension: The name has two endings. The first looks harmless; the last one decides what the file does:
findings.padded: Spaces or underscores in the name push the real ending out of sight.
findings.mismatch: The name’s ending doesn’t match what the file is (see “What it is”):
findings.zipSameName: The archive holds a file and a folder with the same name. WinRAR before version 6.23 ran what was in the folder instead of the file you opened (CVE-2023-38831):
findings.zipTraversal: Some names in the archive point outside the folder you unpack it into:
findings.zipNameMismatch: Some files have one name in the archive’s list and another next to their contents, so different programs show different names:
findings.zipDuplicate: Two files in the archive have the same name, so different programs may open different ones.
findings.hiddenFiles: Some files are marked as hidden, so a file manager won’t show them:
findings.veryHidden: The workbook has sheets hidden so that Excel’s menus can’t show them.
findings.pdfObfuscated: Some of the PDF’s instructions are spelled in a disguised way that hides them from simple checks:
findings.macros: It contains macros: code that runs inside Word, Excel or PowerPoint.
findings.macroSheet: It contains Excel 4.0 macro sheets, an old kind of macro.
findings.activeX: It contains ActiveX controls, which can run code.
findings.dde: It contains a DDE field, which can make Office start another program. If Office asks about updating links or starting an application, say no.
findings.remote: It refers to parts outside the file, which Office may fetch when it opens:
findings.embedded: It contains embedded objects, which can hold any file and run it when double-clicked:
findings.autoUpdate: An embedded object is set to load as soon as the document opens.
findings.equationEditor: It contains an object for the old Equation Editor 3.0, whose flaw attackers have used to run code (CVE-2017-11882).
findings.pdfJavaScript: It contains JavaScript, which PDF readers can run.
findings.pdfAutoAction: It asks the PDF reader to do something by itself: when it opens, or as you move through it.
findings.pdfLaunch: It asks the PDF reader to start a program or open a file:
findings.pdfRemote: It asks the PDF reader to open or read another file:
findings.pdfSubmit: It has a form that sends what you type to an address:
findings.pdfMedia: It contains rich media (Flash or 3D), which some readers can play.
findings.pdfXfa: It contains an XFA form, which can hold scripts.
findings.pageScript: It contains scripts, which run in your browser when the page opens.
findings.passwordForm: It has a password box. Real services don’t send their sign-in pages as attachments. What you type is sent to:
findings.smuggling: It carries another file hidden inside, which the page can save to your device when it opens (HTML smuggling).
findings.refresh: It sends you to another page as soon as it opens:
findings.foreignObject: The picture contains a piece of web page.
findings.remoteFolder: Its working folder is on another computer. A Windows flaw let shortcuts like this run programs from there (CVE-2025-33053):
findings.linkToProgram: It has links that start a program or open a file on another computer instead of a web page:
findings.diskImage: It’s a disk image. Opening it adds a drive to your computer, and the files on it may not carry the mark that brings up warnings about files from the internet.
findings.insideActive: It contains files that can run code:
findings.encrypted: It’s locked with a password, so what it holds couldn’t be checked.
findings.cantList: This tool can’t look inside this kind of file.
findings.tooLarge: It’s too large to look into here: only its name and type were checked.
findings.damaged: It’s damaged or isn’t what its type says, so it couldn’t be read.
findings.partlyRead: Some parts couldn’t be read, so they weren’t checked.
findings.nested: It contains another archive, too deep to open here.
findings.insideLocked: Some files inside couldn’t be fully checked:
findings.webPage: It’s a web page. Opened from a file, it can look like any site, including a sign-in page that sends your password to someone else.
findings.svgPage: It’s an SVG picture. Opened on its own, an SVG works like a web page: it can run scripts and show links.

payloads.webClip: a web shortcut on the Home Screen

kinds.cfb: an older Microsoft Office or Windows file
kinds.unknown: a file this tool doesn’t recognise

attachment.note1: Attachments are one of the oldest ways to attack someone, and they have changed. In Microsoft’s figures for July to September 2026, web pages (HTML, 26–32 %), PDFs (27–30 %) and SVG pictures (13–20 %) carried most of the harmful attachments it saw in email, and 94–96 % of all harmful attachments led to a fake sign-in page rather than installing software. Neither Gmail nor Outlook blocks these types.
attachment.note2: The checker reads what is in the file, not its name: browsers take a file’s type from its ending, so a program renamed “invoice.pdf” still claims to be a PDF. It then looks for what attacks rely on: endings that run a program (from Gmail’s and Outlook’s blocked lists), names that hide the real ending, Office macros, PDF actions, and web pages with scripts or password boxes. ZIP and similar archives, ISO disc images and Outlook messages are opened, and each file in them is checked too.
attachment.note3: On Windows, Office blocks macros in files from the internet and shows a “Security Risk” banner. Removing that block (Properties > Unblock) lets the macros run. Files without the mark that triggers it show an older warning with an Enable content button instead. Files inside disk images and some archives may not carry that mark.
attachment.note4: What it can’t do: it doesn’t know every trick, and it can’t look inside RAR, 7-Zip, CAB, OneNote, VHD, VHDX or DMG files, or password-locked files. It doesn’t open links, so it can’t tell what a page does. “Nothing that runs was found” isn’t a guarantee. If you weren’t expecting a file, contact the sender in another way, not by replying to the message.
attachment.ai1: Uploading a file to an online scanner or an AI service hands the file itself, with everything in it, to whoever runs that service. This tool reads the file on your device instead. In exchange, it doesn’t compare the file with lists of known malware, which online scanners do.

email.title: Email header analyzer
email.summary: Paste an email’s headers to see who really sent it, what your mail provider’s checks found and where replies would go. Nothing is uploaded.
email.description: See who really sent an email, where replies go, and what SPF, DKIM and DMARC found. The headers are read in your browser, never uploaded.
email.input: Paste the headers or the whole message source
email.inputHint: Open the message’s original or source view in your mail program, copy all of it and paste it here. Headers hold your address and your contacts’ addresses; they stay on this device.
email.file: Or choose a saved message (.eml or .msg)
email.example2: Passes every check, still a scam

messages.empty: Paste the headers first, or choose a saved message.
messages.notHeaders: This doesn’t look like email headers. Copy the message’s original or source view, not the text you see when you read it.
messages.tooLarge: This is too large to check here: the limit is about 2 MB of pasted text or a 25 MB file.
messages.msgNoHeaders: This Outlook file holds no received headers. That happens with messages that were never sent, such as drafts.

verdicts.warn: This message has warning signs: {n}. Don’t reply, click or pay until you’ve checked with the sender in another way.
verdicts.unchecked: The sender couldn’t be confirmed: your mail provider’s checks aren’t in what you pasted, or only part of the headers is there.
verdicts.none: No warning signs in the headers. That doesn’t prove the message is honest: it only means it came through the domain it names. Anyone who can send from that domain passes too, including a hacked or free mailbox.

identity.name: Shown name
identity.replyToSame: The same organisation as the address.
identity.replyToOther: A different organisation from the address.
identity.returnPathSame: The same organisation as the address.
identity.returnPathOther: A different organisation. That is ordinary for newsletters and mail services.

email.classInternal: an internal network address (an office, home or provider network)

receiver.named: Recorded by: {id}. If that isn’t your mail provider, don’t rely on this section.
receiver.provider: Recorded by: {id} ({provider}). If that isn’t your mail provider, don’t rely on this section.
receiver.unnamed: These results don’t name who wrote them (Microsoft writes them this way). The server that received the message is called {host}.
receiver.none: Your mail provider’s results aren’t in what you pasted.

meanings.unknown: Not a value this tool knows; shown as written.

spf.pass: The sending server may send mail for the bounce address’s domain. That isn’t the address you see.
spf.fail: The sending server may not send mail for the bounce address’s domain. Forwarding often causes this.
spf.softfail: The bounce address’s domain says this server is probably not allowed to send for it.
spf.neutral: The bounce address’s domain doesn’t say whether this server may send for it.
spf.none: The bounce address’s domain publishes no SPF rules.
spf.temperror: The check couldn’t finish because of a temporary error, usually a DNS lookup problem.
spf.permerror: The domain’s SPF rules couldn’t be read.
spf.policy: SPF would have passed, but the receiving server didn’t accept the result under its own rules.

dkim.pass: A domain signed the message and the signed parts weren’t changed after signing. This says which domain, not that the domain is honest.
dkim.fail: A signature didn’t match: the message was changed after signing, or the signature is wrong. Mailing lists often cause this.
dkim.policy: The receiving server didn’t accept the signature under its own rules, for example because the wrong domain signed.
dkim.temperror: The check couldn’t finish because of a temporary error, usually a DNS lookup problem.
dkim.permerror: The signature couldn’t be checked: it is malformed, or its key wasn’t found.

dmarc.pass: The address you see matches a domain that passed SPF or DKIM.
dmarc.fail: The address you see doesn’t match any domain that passed SPF or DKIM.
dmarc.none: The sender’s domain publishes no DMARC policy.
dmarc.temperror: The check couldn’t finish because of a temporary error, usually a DNS lookup problem.
dmarc.permerror: The domain’s DMARC policy couldn’t be read.
dmarc.bestguesspass: Microsoft: the domain has no DMARC policy, but the check would pass if it had one.

arc.pass: The forwarding record is intact: what earlier handlers recorded can be read. It is only as trustworthy as those handlers.

compauth.softpass: Microsoft’s own combined check passed weakly: Microsoft inferred it rather than the domain’s own records proving it.
compauth.none: Microsoft didn’t run its combined check.

domain.same: About: {domain}, the same organisation as the address you see.
domain.other: About: {domain}, a different organisation from the address you see.

email.claimed: Written before the message reached your provider: could be invented.

filter.cat: The kind of protection that acted on the message.
filter.scl: Spam confidence level. Microsoft says it doesn’t decide what happens to mail in its cloud service.
filter.bcl: Bulk complaint level: the higher it is, the more likely the bulk mail draws complaints.
filter.cip: The address that connected to Microsoft’s server.
filter.ctry: The country or region of that address, as Microsoft worked it out. It may not be where the sender is.
filter.dir: Direction: INB inbound, OUT outbound, INT internal.
filter.sfty: Microsoft added a safety tip: 9.19 domain impersonation, 9.20 user impersonation, 9.25 first contact (often harmless).
filter.x-spam-status: SpamAssassin’s result: Yes means it scored as spam.

sfvValues.sks: Marked as spam by a rule, before filtering.
sfvValues.skb: Marked as spam: the sender is on a blocked list in a policy.
sfvValues.blk: Blocked: the sender is on your Blocked Senders list.
sfvValues.sfe: Allowed: the sender is on your Safe Senders list.
sfvValues.ska: Allowed by an anti-spam policy; filtering was skipped.
sfvValues.ski: Filtering was skipped: the sending server’s IP address is on the IP Allow List.
sfvValues.skn: Filtering was skipped by a mail flow rule.

catValues.ftbp: A blocked file type (common attachments filter).

email.routeHint: From the first server named (top) to your provider (bottom). Times are as each server wrote them.
email.dates: The message says it was written {sent}; your provider received it {received}. The first is the sender’s claim, the second is a fact.

hop.tlsAuth: {with}: encrypted, the sender was signed in
hop.auth: {with}: not encrypted, the sender was signed in
hop.unknown: {with}: not a protocol name this tool knows

email.hopClaimed: Claimed by the sending side: could be invented.

findings.dmarcFail: Your provider’s DMARC check failed for {value}: the address you see isn’t backed by that domain’s own checks. Forwarded mail and mailing lists can fail this way too, but so does a forged sender. Treat the sender as unconfirmed and contact them in another way before you act.
findings.spoofedSender: No check by your provider ties this message to {value}: neither SPF nor DKIM passed for that domain. Anyone can write any From address, so contact the sender in another way before you act.
findings.replyElsewhere: Replies would go to {value}, a different organisation from the address you see. Before you reply, check that address with the sender in another way.
findings.replyElsewhereFree: Replies would go to {value}, a free mailbox, not the organisation in the From address. Scams do this so that the answer reaches them. Check with the sender in another way.
findings.nameIsAddress: The shown name holds another address or domain ({value}) than the real one. Mail apps often show only the name, so the message can look as if it came from there.
findings.lookalikeDomain: The domain {first} looks like the name “{second}” but isn’t its official address. Read the address letter by letter.
findings.lookalikeDomainScript: The domain {first} mixes letters from different alphabets, which can make it look like another name.
findings.nameHidden: Invisible or direction-changing characters are hidden in the name, the address or the subject: {value}. They are used to make text look different from what it is.
findings.severalFrom: The message has more than one sender address ({value}), which an ordinary message doesn’t. Mail apps differ in which one they show.
findings.filterSaidSpam: Your provider’s own filter marked this message ({value}).
findings.dkimLength: A signature by {value} covers only the start of the message: text can be added after signing without breaking it. Don’t trust the end of the message because it was signed.
findings.arcBroken: The forwarding record is broken (ARC says fail): what earlier handlers recorded can’t be relied on.
findings.noChecks: There are no results from your provider’s checks, so the sender can’t be confirmed. The route and the addresses are still shown.
findings.noChecksClaimed: The only check results were written before the message reached your provider, so none of them can be relied on.
findings.noChecksNone: Your provider recorded that it checked nothing for this message.
findings.partial: Only part of the headers seems to be here (no Received lines, or no From). Copy the whole original or source view for a full check.
findings.spfFail: SPF failed for {value}. On its own this often happens to ordinary mail that was forwarded.
findings.spfSoftfail: SPF soft-failed for {value}. On its own this often happens to ordinary mail that was forwarded.
findings.dkimFail: A DKIM signature by {value} didn’t match. Mailing lists that add a footer or change the subject cause this to ordinary mail too.
findings.freeMailbox: The address is at a free mail service ({value}), where anyone can open a mailbox under any name. Check whether the organisation in the name really writes from this address.
findings.signedByOther: The message was signed by {value}, not by the organisation in the From address. A mail service signing its customers’ mail does this; it says nothing about the sender.
findings.fakeReply: The subject looks like a reply (“{value}”), but the message doesn’t refer to an earlier one. Scams do this to look like an ongoing conversation.
findings.dateOdd: The message’s date is far from the time your provider received it.
findings.dateOddFuture: The message’s date is later than the time your provider received it. The date is set by the sender’s device, so it can be wrong or made up.
findings.dateOddOld: The message’s date is more than a week before your provider received it. The date is set by the sender’s device, so it can be wrong or made up.
findings.slowHop: A step on the route took more than an hour (at {value}). Delays happen; on their own they aren’t a warning sign.
findings.backwards: A step on the route has an earlier time than the step before it (at {value}): a server’s clock is wrong.
findings.plainHop: A step between two organisations wasn’t encrypted ({value}), so it could be read on the way.
findings.privateOrigin: The first server on the route got the message from an internal network address ({value}). That is ordinary for mail sent from an office or home network, and the sending side writes this line.
findings.forwarded: The message was forwarded, or passed through a mailing list, on the way. That can make SPF or DKIM fail on ordinary mail.
findings.oldDkim: A signature by {value} uses an outdated method, or had expired when the message arrived.
findings.bulkSender: This is bulk mail: it has an unsubscribe link or a campaign ID. A different bounce address is ordinary here.
findings.mailingList: This came through a mailing list: {value}.
findings.autoReply: The message says it was sent automatically ({value}).
findings.software: The sender’s mail program named itself: {value}.
findings.senderAddress: The message has an X-Originating-IP header with the address {value}. The name suggests the sender’s own connection, but none of the mail services we checked documents it, and the sending side can write anything there.
findings.messageIdElsewhere: The message ID was made at {value}, not at the sender’s domain. Mail services do this for their customers; it is only a hint.
findings.encryptedInTransit: The last step to your provider was encrypted ({value}).
findings.riskyAttachment: An attached file’s name says it can run a program, or hides its real ending: {value}. Don’t open it; if you weren’t expecting it, ask the sender in another way.
findings.remoteImages: Pictures loaded from the internet: {value}. Pictures like these can be used to tell the sender whether you opened the message.

email.limit: This tool reads what your mail provider wrote into the message. It can’t look anything up, and it can’t tell whether a message is honest.
email.note1: Everything is read in your browser. Headers hold your address, your contacts’ addresses and sometimes network addresses, which is a reason not to paste them into a website that receives them. The online analyzers we looked at either don’t say what they do with what you paste, or collect usage data.
email.note2: What a pass means: the receiving server recorded that a domain vouched for the message. That ties the message to a domain, not to a mailbox or a person. A free mailbox anyone can open, or a hacked one, passes every check, and a lookalike domain passes for itself. The standard for these results says so: a pass “does not render the message trustworthy” (RFC 8601).
email.note3: What a failure means: ordinary mail fails too. Forwarding can break SPF, and mailing lists that change a message can break DKIM. DMARC still passes when either one matches the address you see, but forwarded mail and mailing lists can make DMARC fail as well. So a single failed check is only a note here; a failed DMARC check, or no check tying the message to its address, is a warning, because a forged sender looks exactly like that.
email.note4: What it can’t do: it makes no requests, so it can’t look anything up in DNS, verify a signature or check a sender’s reputation. It believes only the lines your own provider wrote at the top of the message; everything below them came with the message and could be invented. It works out organisations from a list built into the site, while the current DMARC standard (RFC 9989, May 2026) looks them up in DNS, so the two can differ; your provider’s own DMARC result is used wherever there is one. How each mail provider writes its headers wasn’t checked against real mail.
email.note5: If a message worries you, don’t reply, click or pay. Contact the sender in a way you already know, not with the details in the message, and report it to your mail provider. The links under the report lead to the steps.
email.ai1: A chatbot can read headers and explain them. Pasting them gives the company behind it your address, your contacts’ addresses and details of the networks the message passed through.
email.ai2: A confident wrong answer about a scam is costly. This tool applies fixed rules, shows which lines it believes and why, and says what it can’t tell.

browser.title: What your browser reveals
browser.summary: See what every website you visit can learn about your device without asking, and try what autofill gives away.
browser.description: See what your browser tells every website: language, time zone, device, graphics chip, fonts and a fingerprint that identifies you without cookies. Shown only to you.
browser.fingerprintWhy: A code made from the details below. Sites can work out a similar code, and it can help them recognise your browser even after you delete cookies. It isn’t unique: identical phones can share it, and it changes when one of the details does.

why.languages: Shows which languages you read, in order of preference.
why.timeZone: Narrows down where you are, even behind a VPN.
why.userAgent: Your browser, its version and your operating system.
why.os: Some browsers give the exact system version when a site asks.
why.gpu: The exact graphics chip often gives away the model of your computer or phone.
why.screen: Size and sharpness differ from device to device.
why.window: The size of the browser window. It changes as you resize it, but at a given moment it narrows down who you are.
why.motion: An accessibility setting. Settings like this can hint at a health condition.
why.dnt: A request not to be tracked. Most sites ignore it.
why.gpc: A newer signal that some privacy laws require sites to respect.
why.canvas: This page drew a small picture out of sight. Each device draws it slightly differently, so the result works like a signature. Some browsers change it on purpose every time.
why.fonts: Fonts show which programs are installed, for example Microsoft Office or design software.
why.referrer: Sites usually see which page sent you. Links from Lockwell don't reveal it.
why.ip: Every website sees your IP address, which shows your internet provider and roughly where you are. To show it here, this page asks Cloudflare, which hosts this site and already sees it with every visit. Nothing is saved.
why.pixelRatio: Changes when you zoom the page, so it is not part of the fingerprint.
why.keyboard: The letters on the first keys show which keyboard layout you use, and so a language. Only Chrome, Edge and similar browsers share it.
why.voices: The voices installed for reading text aloud differ between systems and languages.
why.blocker: Pages can tell whether a content blocker hides elements that look like ads. “Not seen” doesn’t mean you have no blocker: some work on the network instead, where this page can’t see them.

autofill.heading: Try it: what autofill gives away
autofill.intro: Saved names, addresses and phone numbers are handy. But a page can contain fields you can't see, and your browser may fill those in too. Start typing in the name field and choose one of your browser's suggestions.
autofill.name: Name
autofill.leaked: Your browser also filled in fields you couldn't see:
autofill.safe: Nothing extra was filled in. You typed by hand, you have no saved address, or your browser protected you.
autofill.note: This form goes nowhere. What was filled in is shown only here and is erased when you clear it or leave the page. Bank cards are not part of this demonstration.
autofill.tip: To protect yourself, turn off address autofill in your browser's settings, or use a password manager that fills in only when you ask.
autofill.browsersHeading: What browsers do with hidden fields

browsers.firefox: Firefox doesn’t fill fields it can’t see.
browsers.chromium: Chrome, Edge and similar browsers skip fields that can’t be selected, but their code suggests they still fill fields that are only moved out of sight, like the ones here.
browsers.safari: For Safari we found no current statement.
browsers.study: A 2020 study found hidden autofilled fields on hundreds of popular websites.

cannot.heading: What websites can't see without asking
cannot.item1: Your browsing history and your other open tabs.
cannot.item2: Files on your device, unless you choose one yourself.
cannot.item3: Passwords you saved for other sites.
cannot.item4: Your camera, microphone and exact location, until you allow them.
cannot.item5: What you copied, unless you paste it.

browser.note1: None of the details above needs your permission. Each is harmless alone, but together they form a fingerprint that can help sites recognise your browser, even without cookies.
browser.note2: These values are read by this page and shown only to you. They are not sent anywhere. Only if you press the IP button does the page make one request: to this site’s own address /cdn-cgi/trace, which Cloudflare, the host of this site, answers.
browser.note3: You can reduce what sites learn: keep your browser updated, use a browser with fingerprinting protection such as Firefox, Brave or Tor Browser, and remove extensions you don't need.
browser.local: Runs in your browser. Nothing is sent or saved unless you ask: the IP button makes one request to Cloudflare, which hosts this site, and “Remember these values” keeps them in this tab only.
browser.fingerprintProtected: Your browser changed the drawing test on purpose, so this code is likely to be different on other sites or on your next visit. That makes it harder to recognise you by it.
browser.ratingsNote: Ratings show how well each detail told browsers apart in large studies; the thresholds are ours. Time zone and language are rare worldwide but common within one country. Sources:

protected.screen: Your browser reports the window size as the screen size, as Safari’s fingerprinting protection does. A window in full screen looks the same.
protected.timeZone: Tor Browser and Firefox’s strongest protection report this time zone for everyone, unless your device is really set to it.
protected.window: The window size is on a grid of 200 × 100, as Tor Browser and Firefox’s strongest protection make it.
protected.canvas: Your browser changed the drawing on purpose: coloured squares came back slightly different. This value changes, so sites can’t rely on it to recognise you.

steps.heading: What you can do in this browser
steps.firefox: In Firefox, choose Strict tracking protection: it adds protection against fingerprinting, which Private windows have as well. In Tor Browser, change nothing and install no add-ons: its users are meant to look alike, and the Tor Project warns that add-ons can make yours stand out.
steps.safari: Safari’s Advanced Fingerprinting Protection is on in Private Browsing, and can be turned on for all browsing.
steps.brave: Brave changes several of these details for each site and each session while Shields are on. Keep Shields on.
steps.chromium: Chrome and Edge don’t change these details to protect you. Firefox with Strict protection, Brave and Safari do.
steps.other: This page doesn’t know what protection your browser has. Browsers inside apps, like Facebook’s or Telegram’s, usually have none of their own.

compare.heading: Compare after changing a setting
compare.intro: Remember the values above, change a setting in your browser, then reload this page: what changed is marked. The values are kept only in this tab. Press Forget them when you’re done: a browser that restores closed tabs may bring them back.
compare.remembered: Remembered. Change a setting, then reload this page.
compare.failed: This browser doesn’t let the page keep them, even in this tab.
compare.same: Nothing changed since you remembered them.

browser.ipFailed: Couldn’t get it. A content blocker may have stopped the request, or this copy of the site isn’t served through Cloudflare, which answers it.

check.title: Link checker
check.summary: Paste a link you're not sure about and see which site it really points to, before you open it.
check.description: Check a suspicious link without opening it: see the real site it leads to and the tricks phishing links use, such as look-alike letters and fake brand names.
check.input: Paste a link, or the message it came in
check.invalid: No web link was found. A link looks like https://example.com/page or example.com/page.
check.ok: No warning signs in the address. That doesn't prove the site is safe: if you weren't expecting this link, don't open it.

warnings.redirect: The link first goes through {via}, which then sends you on to {site}.
warnings.http: The connection is not encrypted (http instead of https). Don't type a password or card number there.
warnings.ip: The address is a number instead of a name. Real services almost never send links like this.
warnings.userinfo: There is an “@” in the address. Everything before it is decoration; the real site is {site}.
warnings.port: The address uses an unusual port number ({port}).
warnings.mixedScript: The name mixes alphabets, for example Latin and Cyrillic letters that look the same. This is a classic way to fake a well-known address.
warnings.lookalikeScript: The name is written in letters from another alphabet that look just like English ones.
warnings.brandSubdomain: “{brand}” appears at the start of the address, but the site is really {site}. Only the end of the address counts.
warnings.nestedDomain: The address starts with “{inner}”, which looks like another site's address, but the site is really {site}. Only the end of the address counts.
warnings.brandLookalike: The address contains “{brand}”, but {site} is not that company's usual address.
warnings.typo: The address looks like “{brand}” with a small change. Compare it letter by letter.
warnings.shortener: This is a shortened link. It hides the real address, which this tool can't see without opening it.
warnings.deepSubdomain: The address has many parts in front of the site name, which can be used to hide where it leads.
warnings.fileTld: The address ends in .{ending}, which looks like a file type. It is a website, not a file.
warnings.download: The link points to a file that can install or run software (.{file}). Open it only if you were expecting it.
warnings.textMismatch: The link's text shows {shown}, but the link leads to {site}. This is the clearest sign of a fake link.
warnings.brandElsewhere: {site} is not the address of “{brand}”, which is {official}. It may belong to an unrelated company with the same name, or to someone imitating it.
warnings.latinLookalike: The name uses letters that only look like ordinary ones (for example “ı” without a dot) to pass for “{brand}”.
warnings.sharedHost: {site} is a page on {suffix}, where anyone can make one for free. Whoever made the page chose the name in front of {suffix}; it says nothing about who they are.
warnings.brandPath: The address of “{brand}” appears after the site name, but the link leads to {site}. Only the site name counts.
warnings.carriedUrl: The link carries another address inside it ({carried}). Sites do this to send you on after a step; scams do it to pass you to their own page.
warnings.carriedEmail: The link contains an email address ({email}). Opening it can tell the sender that this address is real and read.
warnings.hiddenTarget: The link passes through {via}, a mail security service that keeps the real address on its own servers. This tool can't see where it leads. Ask the sender for the address itself, or open the site yourself.
warnings.mailTracking: The link passes through {via}, a mailing service that counts clicks and keeps the real address on its own servers. This tool can’t see where it leads. If you don’t know the sender, open the site yourself instead.
warnings.publicPage: Anyone can publish a page, form or file on {page}. The site’s name says nothing about who made this page.

check.note1: Read an address from the end. In login.example.com.evil.ge the site is evil.ge; everything in front of it can be anything the owner likes, including the name of your bank.
check.note2: The tool reads only the text of the link. It never opens it and never contacts the site, so nobody learns that you checked. For the same reason it can't know what the page contains.
check.note3: A clean result is not a guarantee. When a message asks you to log in or pay, don't use its link: open the site yourself from a bookmark or by typing the address.
check.several: The text has {n} links. Each one is checked below.
check.ai1: You can ask an AI chatbot whether a link is safe, but treat the answer with care. Many can't open the page at all and still answer confidently; others are fooled by the same tricks that fool people. This tool does one narrow thing reliably: it reads the address itself, by fixed rules, and shows where it leads. And if a suspicious link came in a private message, pasting the whole message into a chatbot shares that conversation too.
check.exampleText: GPost: your parcel is held at customs. Pay the 1.99 GEL fee within 24 hours: gpost-ge.info/pay?id=GE4471 Or sign in to your bank here: https://tbc-login.pages.dev/auth
check.qr: Or read a QR code from a picture
check.qrHint: Choose a photo or screenshot of the QR code. The picture stays on your device; the tool reads the link in it without opening it.
check.qrNone: No QR code was found in this picture. Try a sharper photo, taken straight on.
check.qrFailed: This browser couldn't read the picture.

scheme.data: This is a “data:” address: the page is packed inside the link itself instead of coming from a website. Ordinary links never look like this. Don't open it.
scheme.javascript: This is a “javascript:” address: opening it runs a program in the page you are on. Ordinary links never look like this. Don't open it.
scheme.other: This is not a web address, so this tool can't check it. Links to websites start with https:// or http://.

check.capped: The text has {n} links. The first {max} are checked below; check the rest separately.
check.ascii: The browser sends this name as {host}.
check.defanged: This address was written in a disarmed form (such as hxxps or [.]) and is read here as a normal address.
check.qrAbsent: This browser can’t read QR codes from pictures. Point your phone’s camera at the code and type the address it shows here, without opening it.

redact.title: Image redaction
redact.summary: Cover faces, names or messages in a photo or screenshot with solid shapes, crop away the rest, and save a copy that hides them for good.
redact.description: Cover faces, names, number plates or messages in a photo or screenshot with solid shapes, and crop it, before sharing. Works in your browser: the image is never uploaded.
redact.pasteHint: You can also paste a screenshot or drop a file here.
redact.canvas: Your image. Drag to cover what should be hidden.
redact.help: Drag on the image to cover an area. Tap a covered area to select it, then drag it to move it or drag its handles to resize it. Use two fingers to move around a zoomed image. With a keyboard: focus the image, press Enter to add an area, move it with the arrow keys, resize it with Shift and the arrow keys, remove it with Delete, and switch between areas with Page Up and Page Down. Without dragging: Add area puts a box in the middle, and the buttons under the image move and resize the selected area.
redact.cropped: Only the outlined part will be in the copy.
redact.resultHelp: This is exactly the picture that will be saved. Look for anything that can still be read or recognised.
redact.verified: Checked: the saved file was read back, and every pixel inside the covered areas is black.
redact.verifiedJpeg: Checked: the saved file was read back, and every pixel inside the covered areas is black, apart from a border 2 pixels wide that JPEG softens.
redact.verifiedThin: Some areas are too thin to check this way: look at them closely yourself.
redact.verifiedEmpty: Nothing is covered in this copy: it shows the picture as it is.
redact.verifyFailed: The saved file didn't pass the check: some covered areas aren't solid black, so it isn't offered. Try again, or use another browser.
redact.verifyBlocked: This browser doesn't let the page read the picture back, so the copy couldn't be checked and isn't offered. Tor Browser, Mullvad Browser and Firefox with fingerprinting protection block this: allow this site to read canvas data (usually from an icon in the address bar), then check again.
redact.copyFailed: This browser can't copy images. Save the copy instead.
redact.unsupported: This file can't be opened as an image. Choose a JPEG, PNG or WebP file.
redact.tooLarge: This file is too large. The limit is 40 MB.
redact.resized: The image is very large, so the saved copy is scaled down to {w} × {h}.
redact.encodeFailed: The browser could not create the copy. Try a smaller image.
redact.animated: This picture is animated. Only its first frame is shown here and saved.
redact.replaceText: Open the new picture? What you covered in this one hasn't been saved and will be lost.
redact.note1: Covered areas are solid and painted into the picture itself. In the saved copy the pixels underneath no longer exist, so nobody can uncover them. This tool doesn't blur on purpose: blurred text and faces can sometimes be recovered.
redact.note2: The saved copy is a new picture, so it carries none of the original's hidden data such as location, date and device. Parts you crop away are not in the copy at all.
redact.note3: The image is opened in your browser only. It is not uploaded, and this site can't see it.
redact.note4: Look at the result before you share it. Cover reflections, name tags, tattoos, street signs and screens too, and remember that the original is still on your device.
redact.note5: The size of a box hints at what is under it: a short box over a name suggests a short name. Cover more than the word itself, for example the whole line.
redact.ai1: AI image editors can now hide a face or erase a name too, often more neatly than a black box. The catch is how they do it: to change the picture, the service has to receive the original, with everything you wanted hidden still in it.
redact.ai2: Most AI services keep what you upload for some time, and some let staff look at it or use it to train future models, depending on your settings and plan. For a picture you are covering precisely because it is sensitive, that defeats the purpose. An AI that “removes” something also fills the gap with invented detail, which someone may later take for the real thing. A plain black shape drawn on your own device is less elegant, but nothing leaves the device and nobody can mistake it for the original.

editor.title: Photo editor
editor.summary: Crop, straighten, resize and correct a photo, add text or drawings, and save it as JPEG, PNG or WebP. It all happens in your browser: the photo is never uploaded.
editor.description: Crop, straighten, resize and correct a photo, add text and drawings, and save it as JPEG, PNG or WebP, in your browser. The photo is never uploaded.
editor.pasteHint: You can also paste a screenshot or drop a file here.
editor.canvas: Your photo. What dragging does depends on the tool you chose.
editor.help: Choose a tool to see its controls: beside the photo on a large screen, under it on a phone. To crop, drag the frame or its edges; with Text or Draw, tap an item to select it. Use two fingers to move around a zoomed photo. With a keyboard: focus the photo; the arrow keys move the crop frame or the selected item, Shift and the arrow keys resize it, Delete removes it, + and − zoom, and Ctrl+Z (⌘Z on a Mac) undoes. Without dragging: every tool has buttons and fields that do the same.

editor.blocked: This browser doesn’t let the page read back the picture it draws, so a saved copy could hold made-up pixels and none is offered. Some browsers, such as Tor Browser, do this to protect against fingerprinting: allow this site to read canvas data (usually from an icon in the address bar), then open the photo again.
editor.replaceText: Open the new picture? Your changes to this one haven’t been saved and will be lost.
editor.redactLink: To hide a face or a name, use {link}: it covers them with solid shapes.
editor.filtersHelp: A filter works together with the sliders under Adjust.
editor.drawHelp: Drag on the photo to draw. Tap something you drew or wrote to select it: drag it to move it, drag a corner to resize it, or drag the round handle to turn it. With a keyboard: focus the photo, press Enter to add, move the selected item with the arrow keys, resize it with Shift and the arrow keys, switch between items with Page Up and Page Down, and remove it with Delete.
editor.selectedNone: Nothing selected. Tap an item on the photo, or add one.
editor.note1: The photo is opened and edited in your browser only. It is never uploaded, so it doesn’t reach this site’s server.
editor.note2: The saved copy is a new picture drawn from the photo’s pixels, so it carries none of the original’s hidden file data, such as the place, the date or the camera model. What the picture shows can still give these away, and experts can sometimes tell which camera took a photo from faint traces its sensor leaves in the pixels. The copy can include a colour profile and similar details, which describe the picture, not you. The original file on your device still has its hidden data.
editor.note3: This editor has no tool for hiding or blurring part of a picture. “Soften the whole photo” changes the look of all of it and is not for hiding: blurred text can sometimes be read back, and blurred faces can sometimes be recognised. To hide a face, a name or a number plate, use Image redaction, which covers them with solid shapes.
editor.note4: JPEG suits photos and makes small files, but it drops some detail to do so, and a lower quality drops more. PNG keeps every pixel, so it suits screenshots and text. WebP files are often smaller still, but Safari and most browsers on iPhone and iPad can’t write them, so the option is switched off there. Keep the original if you may need it again.
editor.note5: Very large pictures are scaled down to what a browser can handle, and an animated picture keeps only its first frame. The editor works in the standard sRGB colour range: a photo with a wider range of colours is converted, so its most vivid colours may look a little duller.
editor.ai1: AI photo editors can do things this tool can’t, such as removing a background or an object, or filling in an edge. To change the picture, the service has to receive it, unless the app says the work is done on your device. If the photo is sent as it is, its hidden data, which can include the place it was taken, goes with it.
editor.ai2: What happens to an upload afterwards depends on the service and your settings, so read what it says about keeping files and using them to train models. AI tools also invent detail when they fill in or enlarge a picture, and someone may later take it for the real thing. Cropping, correcting colours and adding text need nothing of the kind: here nothing leaves your device.

document.description: Check the hidden details in DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, ODT, ODS, ODP or PDF files: authors, comment and change authors, paths, printer, earlier versions and more. Save a cleaned copy. Nothing is uploaded.

document.note1: Office programs and PDF exporters write your name, your organisation, the software and the dates into every file. Sources have been identified from these details.
document.note2: The document is opened in your browser only. It is not uploaded, and this site can't see it.
document.note3: For Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OpenDocument files the clean copy has its properties emptied; the names on comments and tracked changes replaced with “Author” and their dates removed; the template’s location, the saved folder, printer names, document IDs and editing-session numbers removed; signatures, co-authoring records and the preview picture removed; and hidden data stripped from photos inside. The text, formatting and pictures themselves are not touched. Before offering the copy, the tool reads it again and searches it for every name, path and ID it found.
document.note4: What a clean copy can still reveal: the comments and tracked changes themselves, names typed in the text, hidden sheets and slides, and everything listed under “Found and left in” or “Could not be checked”. For anything sensitive, copy the text into a new, empty document.
document.dropHint: You can choose or drop several files at once.
document.ai1: It is tempting to hand a document to an AI assistant and ask it to make it anonymous or to look for hidden details. Doing so sends the whole document, text and properties alike, to that company's servers, where it may be kept and, depending on your settings and plan, read by staff or used to train models. Check and clean a document you want to protect on your own device first, and think twice about what you upload after that.

hidden.title: Hidden character detector
hidden.summary: Paste text to reveal invisible characters and look-alike letters that can be used to trace who shared it.
hidden.description: Find invisible characters, unusual spaces and look-alike letters hidden in a text, which can mark a copy and reveal who leaked it. Get a clean version. Nothing is sent anywhere.
hidden.none: No hidden or unusual characters found.
hidden.truncated: Only the first 2,000 places are shown below. The count and the clean text cover the whole text.
hidden.markHint: Tap or click a marked place to see what was found there.

flags.zeroWidth: Characters with no width: the usual way to hide a mark inside text
flags.bidi: Marks that change the direction of text, also used to disguise file names and links
flags.tags: Invisible characters that can carry a whole hidden message
flags.softHyphen: Hyphens that only appear at a line break
flags.spaces: Spaces of a different width from the ordinary one; a pattern of them can identify a copy
flags.trailing: Spaces or tabs at the end of lines, which nobody sees
flags.lookalike: Words that mix alphabets, such as a Cyrillic “а” in an English word, and whole words written in another alphabet whose letters all look like the text’s own. They are not changed in the clean text: check them yourself
flags.doubleSpace: Two or more spaces between words. Some people type them out of habit, but varying them is also a simple way to make one copy differ from another
flags.quotes: Straight and curly quotation marks or apostrophes are mixed. Copies made for different people can differ in exactly this
flags.dashes: Hyphens that look the same but are different characters, such as a non-breaking hyphen or a minus sign beside ordinary hyphens
flags.fullwidth: Wide forms of Latin letters and digits, made for Chinese and Japanese text. Elsewhere they make a copy differ while looking almost the same
flags.mathLetters: Letters that look bold or italic but are really mathematical symbols. Search, screen readers and spell checkers don’t read them as words
flags.compatibility: Symbols that stand in for ordinary letters or punctuation, such as the ligature ﬁ, the Roman numeral ⅰ or the Greek question mark
flags.composition: The same accented letter is stored as one character in some places and as a letter plus an accent in others. Both look identical; with the box above ticked, the clean text stores them one way
flags.dotless: The Turkish letter ı, which looks almost like i, inside a word in another language
flags.georgianCase: Georgian capital letters (Mtavruli) mixed into a word in ordinary letters. Georgian doesn’t use capitals inside a word, so this marks the text

hidden.note1: A document can be marked so that every copy is slightly different: an invisible character here, a wider space there, a letter swapped for its twin from another alphabet. If the text leaks, the pattern shows whose copy it was.
hidden.note2: The clean text has invisible characters removed and unusual spaces replaced with ordinary ones; tick the box above to also make spacing, quotes and letter forms uniform. A mark made with wording, such as a changed word or comma, can’t be found in a single copy, and neither can a letter swapped for a look-alike from the same alphabet, such as a lowercase l for a capital I. With two copies of the same text, “Compare two copies” shows every difference. For something sensitive, retell it in your own words.
hidden.note3: The text stays in your browser. It is not sent or saved.
hidden.ai1: Invisible characters matter for AI in two ways. First, a text can carry hidden instructions that you can't see but an AI assistant will read. If you paste such a text, or let an assistant read a web page or an email that contains it, the assistant may follow those instructions instead of yours. The “hidden tag characters” above are the usual carrier. Check text from a source you don't trust before you give it to an assistant.
hidden.ai2: Second, text written by AI tools sometimes arrives with unusual spaces or invisible characters of its own. Not every such character is a deliberate mark, but the clean text removes them either way. Watermarks that work through the choice of words, which some companies are developing, can't be seen or removed by this tool.
